REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] This is the decision in the claims of XXXX XXXX(the principal claimant), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX(the female claimant) and their two sons, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX(minor claimants) - nationals of Hungary who are claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the Act). The principal claimant fears a criminal element he calls "mafia" and one mafia member in particular who extorted him; he also fears what they would do to him and his family if the claimants returned to Hungary.

[2] The panel heard these claims jointly pursuant to Rule 55 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.2 In addition, the Act requires the designation of a representative for all claimants less than 18 years of age.3 For the purposes of the claim for refugee protection, in accordance with subsection 167(2) of the Act, the panel appointed the principal claimant to be the Designated Representative for his two sons, the minor claimants.
ALLEGATIONS

[3] The principal claimant's experiences are set out in the narrative portion of his Personal Information Form (PIF)4 and in the amended narrative5. The other claimants rely on the narrative set out in the principal claimant's PIF. The claimants fear returning to Hungary because they fear mafia elements that have extorted money from their business.
The Evidence

[4] Summarily, the principal claimant and his family lived in Délegyháza, Hungary, a village in Pest County located south of Budapest. The principal claimant and his wife were gainfully employed throughout their adult lives. In XXXX 2010, the principal claimant opened his business XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX and XXXX to business chains. The principal claimant's supplier for these products was a company called XXXX XXXX XXXX. A man named XXXX XXXX XXXX, who worked for XXXX XXXX and who represented this supplier, pressured the principal claimant to start paying him 20% of the retail price on each item the principal claimant XXXX. The principal claimant said XXXX was part of the mafia and he wrote that it is common practice for the mafia and other criminal types to register companies' names to homeless persons and then use these registered companies in order to run their businesses. When the principal claimant refused to pay the protection money to XXXX, men came to the claimants' house to 'abuse and threaten' them and the men began to show up at their house "everyday".

[5] The principal claimant's narrative also indicates that XXXX forced him to do a bank transfer and hand over the money to a man that XXXX sent with the principal claimant to the bank. In XXXX 2012, the principal claimant alleged that he was forced to register one of the criminals on his bank account so that he could not do his own banking and in order for the mafia to be able to access and monitor his account. He later recanted this information in his 'PIF Narrative Addition'6. When the principal claimant tried to get help from the police station in nearby Ráczkeve, a couple of mafia men were watching him from a car as he left the station. They threatened the principal claimant with a gun and hit him multiple times and warned him that they had high-ranking police connections. The claimants received a 'one week respite', presumably to come up with extortion money, that ended on XXXX XXXX 2012. The next day, the claimants rented a car and drove to Germany to stay with the female claimant's sister. The criminals called the principal claimant and threatened him and they put a bounty on him of 8 million Hungarian Forints (roughly C$38,000). The claimants came to Canada on 7 September 2012 and filed refugee claims.

[6] The principal claimant's aforementioned 'PIF Narrative Addition' indicates that he sent a request to the police in Ráczkeve asking them to confirm that he had been to the station in XXXX 2012, adding that they had refused to help him when he went to the station on that occasion. He has not received a reply to that request. The principal claimant said he paid the protection money from XXXX2012 to XXXX2012 but his added narrative indicates that no other person was registered on his bank account and that he left Hungary on XXXX XXXX 2012. He wrote that the demand to access his bank account was made at the end of XXXX 2012, but he later clarified that in fact no other person was registered on his bank account. The female claimant's daughter XXXX - a woman who did not accompany the claimants to Germany and who still lives in Hungary - called the claimants in Germany to say that some of these mafia types had been looking for the principal claimant and they told her that they had placed a bounty on the principal claimant. The principal claimant wrote in the 'PIF Narrative Addition' narrative that the reference he made to the criminals phoning him in Germany was a misunderstanding. The female claimant's daughter also reported that the same mafia people went to the home of the principal claimant's mother to look for him. The principal claimant wrote that it was then that he threw away his cellphone. In early 2013, mafia people went back to the mother's home, as well as to the adult daughter's home, to make the same demand, to know where the principal claimant was. In Canada, the claimants learned that the mafia offered the principal claimant's mother 5 million Forints for information that would help them find the claimants. The principal claimant wrote that his 17-year-old son XXXX has been emotionally affected by these experiences and that he was hospitalized in Canada in XXXX 2017 after a suicide attempt.
DETERMINATION

[7] The panel determines that there is no nexus between the claimants' allegations and any of the Convention grounds. The claimants do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary for a Convention ground. Further, the panel finds that they are not persons in need of protection as their removal to Hungary would not subject them personally to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture.
IDENTITY

Criminality per se provides no nexus to a Convention ground and does not permit the panel to find that these claimants are Convention refugees. The principal claimant is effectively alleging a fear of criminal reprisals or a criminal vendetta with a bounty placed on his head by the mafia according to his wife's adult daughter. However, as victims of criminal vendettas do not constitute a particular social group as per the Ward8 decision, the claimants cannot benefit from Convention refugee protection.

[11] As the principal claimant alleges that the reason for his claim is that he was targeted for extortion by the mafia, one of whom he can name (XXXX), and as the state is not the agent of persecution, the torture ground is not available to these claimants. The panel finds that the adult claimants' fear of harm does not have a nexus to the Convention refugee definition. The panel is also not persuaded that what the claimants fear amounts to persecution or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. Thus, the panel assessed the claimants' allegations under section 97(1) of the Act. Specifically, the panel considered whether the risk that the adult claimants and their two sons face in Hungary is one which is faced generally by other individuals in that country, pursuant to section 97(1)(b)(ii) of the Act.

[12] The principal claimant complied with XXXX demands for money until the money ran out at the end of XXXX in 2012 at which time he decided to close his business and leave Hungary. Based on what he alleges, his wife's adult daughter said to him on the phone, the criminals threatened to put a bounty on the principal claimant's head. Even if the panel were to accept this element as true, the principal claimant's fear here appears to be speculative at best - based on something his wife's daughter told him over the phone - and constitutes no more than a fear of generalized violence. The panel also does not believe the principal claimant's claim that he is wanted today by the man from his supplier's company, or by other related mafia types. More than five years have passed since the principal claimant closed his XXXX XXXX XXXX and left Hungary. He is no longer a businessman in his hometown; in that he no longer operates a business there. While living in Hungary, the principal claimant allegedly paid the money to XXXX and his cohorts for around six months until he testified that he could no longer afford to do so. As a result of this development he left the country. It is implausible to the panel that a bounty was placed on him, as his wife's daughter told him on the phone. The principal claimant had paid the requested money to XXXX for nearly half a year until he decided he could no longer do so. Having left the country, it is implausible that XXXX and his cohorts would continue to be interested in the principal claimant. If XXXX is the corrupt man the principal claimant alleges he is, it is more likely that XXXX would simply find other small business owners in the area to target for money; not these claimants who have no business and who by their own admission have no further ties to Hungary, and who left the country more than five years ago. Moreover, the principal claimant was never a rich man and testified that he has nothing left today and would have no means to support his family if he returned to Hungary. The principal claimant's economic situation upon return to Hungary is not a factor in assessing the grounds for refugee status and the panel finds no basis for the principal claimant's fear, or risk of harm from criminal elements, all these years after closing his small business - a business that consisted of himself as the sole employee driving supplies around to his clients using the family car.

[15] The panel finds that the objective documentary evidence and the testimony of the minor claimant XXXX do not support the principal claimant's allegation. In marked contrast to the principal claimant's testimony, XXXX testified on his own behalf regarding the cause of the mental and emotional issues he faced leading up to his attempted suicide in late XXXX 2017. He told the counsel and the panel that he had 'medical issues' before being hospitalized in XXXX, although he had never previously sought professional help. He attributed his problems to pressure he was experiencing in school in Canada and specifically, to the pressure he was placing on himself to do well in school. He said that he was doing 'a lot more tests' in chemistry, biology, mathematics and English and the pressure he was experiencing was such that he dropped all of his school subjects. He was clear with the panel and his counsel when he stated that the school work and pressure he put on himself became too much, resulting in his suicide attempt. He said he felt a 'whole load of pressure' lifted off his shoulders after he dropped the courses.

[16] By extension, neither of the medical documents submitted to corroborate XXXX personal situation10 link the reason for his mental collapse to his father's alleged business trouble in Hungary with mafia types trying to extort money from him. For example, the doctor's discharge diagnosis is "Social anxiety disorder, ADD, rule out learning disability." The doctor also referenced XXXX "unrestricted access to video gaming interfering with sleep onset and sleep maintenance" as a factor in treating the boy during his hospitalization. The reporting doctor also noted he took a family history from the two adult claimants and noted that XXXX screening testing came back "clinically significant for ADD." Further, the doctor opined in his report that he is "not certain if anxiety is free-standing social anxiety or actually comorbid or untreated ADD; however, focus of this admission will be treatment of anxiety". Moreover, the doctor recorded the minor claimant's reference to "years of introverted coping style, insecurities, social phobias, social avoidance and isolation." Such diagnoses clearly pre-date any reference to the principal claimant's allegations of several incidents that compelled him to close his business and leave Hungary. In fact, there is no persuasive evidence before the panel - including in the medical evidence - that links XXXX medical issues to what the principal claimant experienced. The panel prefers the medical evidence and XXXX own admission as to the reasons for his medical issues to that of the principal claimant who, the panel finds, sought to use the young man's attempted suicide and hospitalization in XXXX 2017 to establish a subjective fear of criminal elements in Hungary. The panel is not persuaded by the principal claimant's evidence as stated. Further, XXXX testified that he would feel worse if he returned to Hungary as the health care in Hungary is not as good as Canada's health care system. He said he would feel even more depressed and anxious especially since he is accustomed to life in Canada. At no time during the hearing did he offer evidence that his situation stems from any issues that his father and/or the family faced in Hungary.

[27] One of the leading cases on this matter is Portillo21, in which the Federal Court articulated a two-step test for determining generalized versus personalized test. The Board must first appropriately determine the nature of the risk faced by the claimant, which requires an assessment of whether the claimant faces an ongoing or future risk, what that risk is, whether it is one of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and the basis for the risk. Second, the correctly described risk faced by the claimant must then be compared to that faced by a significant group in the country at issue to determine whether the risks are of the same nature and degree. As well, it will typically be the case that where an individual is subject to a personal risk to his life or risks cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, then that risk is no longer general.

[28] In this context, the panel finds that the harm faced by XXXX is not demonstrative of a personalized risk that lies outside of generalized risk faced by others in Hungary. First, the panel considered carefully the best interests of the affected minor claimant XXXX as a person who has experienced, and who has been treated for, mental health issues. The panel considered the medical reports and the minor claimant's current restorative treatment regimen with, among other things, medication and social worker interaction and in the context of his straightforward testimony. None of this evidence or testimony references criminal experiences or the principal claimant's alleged run-ins with the mafia in Hungary. Unlike the decision of Kanthasamy22 as the counsel referenced as being applicable, the panel distinguishes the case at bar from that case. REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] This is the decision in the claims of XXXX XXXX(the principal claimant), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX(the female claimant) and their two sons, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX(minor claimants) - nationals of Hungary who are claiming refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (the Act). The principal claimant fears a criminal element he calls "mafia" and one mafia member in particular who extorted him; he also fears what they would do to him and his family if the claimants returned to Hungary.

[2] The panel heard these claims jointly pursuant to Rule 55 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules.2 In addition, the Act requires the designation of a representative for all claimants less than 18 years of age.3 For the purposes of the claim for refugee protection, in accordance with subsection 167(2) of the Act, the panel appointed the principal claimant to be the Designated Representative for his two sons, the minor claimants.
ALLEGATIONS

[3] The principal claimant's experiences are set out in the narrative portion of his Personal Information Form (PIF)4 and in the amended narrative5. The other claimants rely on the narrative set out in the principal claimant's PIF. The claimants fear returning to Hungary because they fear mafia elements that have extorted money from their business.
The Evidence

[4] Summarily, the principal claimant and his family lived in Délegyháza, Hungary, a village in Pest County located south of Budapest. The principal claimant and his wife were gainfully employed throughout their adult lives. In XXXX 2010, the principal claimant opened his business XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX and XXXX to business chains. The principal claimant's supplier for these products was a company called XXXX XXXX XXXX. A man named XXXX XXXX XXXX, who worked for XXXX XXXX and who represented this supplier, pressured the principal claimant to start paying him 20% of the retail price on each item the principal claimant XXXX. The principal claimant said XXXX was part of the mafia and he wrote that it is common practice for the mafia and other criminal types to register companies' names to homeless persons and then use these registered companies in order to run their businesses. When the principal claimant refused to pay the protection money to XXXX, men came to the claimants' house to 'abuse and threaten' them and the men began to show up at their house "everyday".

[5] The principal claimant's narrative also indicates that XXXX forced him to do a bank transfer and hand over the money to a man that XXXX sent with the principal claimant to the bank. In XXXX 2012, the principal claimant alleged that he was forced to register one of the criminals on his bank account so that he could not do his own banking and in order for the mafia to be able to access and monitor his account. He later recanted this information in his 'PIF Narrative Addition'6. When the principal claimant tried to get help from the police station in nearby Ráczkeve, a couple of mafia men were watching him from a car as he left the station. They threatened the principal claimant with a gun and hit him multiple times and warned him that they had high-ranking police connections. The claimants received a 'one week respite', presumably to come up with extortion money, that ended on XXXX XXXX 2012. The next day, the claimants rented a car and drove to Germany to stay with the female claimant's sister. The criminals called the principal claimant and threatened him and they put a bounty on him of 8 million Hungarian Forints (roughly C$38,000). The claimants came to Canada on 7 September 2012 and filed refugee claims.

[6] The principal claimant's aforementioned 'PIF Narrative Addition' indicates that he sent a request to the police in Ráczkeve asking them to confirm that he had been to the station in XXXX 2012, adding that they had refused to help him when he went to the station on that occasion. He has not received a reply to that request. The principal claimant said he paid the protection money from XXXX2012 to XXXX2012 but his added narrative indicates that no other person was registered on his bank account and that he left Hungary on XXXX XXXX 2012. He wrote that the demand to access his bank account was made at the end of XXXX 2012, but he later clarified that in fact no other person was registered on his bank account. The female claimant's daughter XXXX - a woman who did not accompany the claimants to Germany and who still lives in Hungary - called the claimants in Germany to say that some of these mafia types had been looking for the principal claimant and they told her that they had placed a bounty on the principal claimant. The principal claimant wrote in the 'PIF Narrative Addition' narrative that the reference he made to the criminals phoning him in Germany was a misunderstanding. The female claimant's daughter also reported that the same mafia people went to the home of the principal claimant's mother to look for him. The principal claimant wrote that it was then that he threw away his cellphone. In early 2013, mafia people went back to the mother's home, as well as to the adult daughter's home, to make the same demand, to know where the principal claimant was. In Canada, the claimants learned that the mafia offered the principal claimant's mother 5 million Forints for information that would help them find the claimants. The principal claimant wrote that his 17-year-old son XXXX has been emotionally affected by these experiences and that he was hospitalized in Canada in XXXX 2017 after a suicide attempt.
DETERMINATION

[7] The panel determines that there is no nexus between the claimants' allegations and any of the Convention grounds. The claimants do not have a well-founded fear of persecution in Hungary for a Convention ground. Further, the panel finds that they are not persons in need of protection as their removal to Hungary would not subject them personally to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture.
IDENTITY

[8] The panel finds the claimants to have established their identities as citizens of Hungary based on their oral testimony and photocopies of their national identity documents contained in the Minister's information7 on the Board's file.
ISSUE

[9] The central issues are whether the claimants face a serious possibility of persecution in Hungary for a Convention ground and whether the risk they might face if they return to Hungary is a personalized risk or a generalized risk.
ANALYSIS
Criminality and Nexus to a Convention Ground

[10] The principal claimant's concern is that he is a victim of criminality. Criminality per se provides no nexus to a Convention ground and does not permit the panel to find that these claimants are Convention refugees. The principal claimant is effectively alleging a fear of criminal reprisals or a criminal vendetta with a bounty placed on his head by the mafia according to his wife's adult daughter. However, as victims of criminal vendettas do not constitute a particular social group as per the Ward8 decision, the claimants cannot benefit from Convention refugee protection.

[11] As the principal claimant alleges that the reason for his claim is that he was targeted for extortion by the mafia, one of whom he can name (XXXX), and as the state is not the agent of persecution, the torture ground is not available to these claimants. The panel finds that the adult claimants' fear of harm does not have a nexus to the Convention refugee definition. The panel is also not persuaded that what the claimants fear amounts to persecution or to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture. Thus, the panel assessed the claimants' allegations under section 97(1) of the Act. Specifically, the panel considered whether the risk that the adult claimants and their two sons face in Hungary is one which is faced generally by other individuals in that country, pursuant to section 97(1)(b)(ii) of the Act.

[12] The principal claimant complied with XXXX demands for money until the money ran out at the end of XXXX in 2012 at which time he decided to close his business and leave Hungary. Based on what he alleges, his wife's adult daughter said to him on the phone, the criminals threatened to put a bounty on the principal claimant's head. Even if the panel were to accept this element as true, the principal claimant's fear here appears to be speculative at best - based on something his wife's daughter told him over the phone - and constitutes no more than a fear of generalized violence. The panel also does not believe the principal claimant's claim that he is wanted today by the man from his supplier's company, or by other related mafia types. More than five years have passed since the principal claimant closed his XXXX XXXX XXXX and left Hungary. He is no longer a businessman in his hometown; in that he no longer operates a business there. While living in Hungary, the principal claimant allegedly paid the money to XXXX and his cohorts for around six months until he testified that he could no longer afford to do so. As a result of this development he left the country. It is implausible to the panel that a bounty was placed on him, as his wife's daughter told him on the phone. The principal claimant had paid the requested money to XXXX for nearly half a year until he decided he could no longer do so. Having left the country, it is implausible that XXXX and his cohorts would continue to be interested in the principal claimant. If XXXX is the corrupt man the principal claimant alleges he is, it is more likely that XXXX would simply find other small business owners in the area to target for money; not these claimants who have no business and who by their own admission have no further ties to Hungary, and who left the country more than five years ago. Moreover, the principal claimant was never a rich man and testified that he has nothing left today and would have no means to support his family if he returned to Hungary. The principal claimant's economic situation upon return to Hungary is not a factor in assessing the grounds for refugee status and the panel finds no basis for the principal claimant's fear, or risk of harm from criminal elements, all these years after closing his small business - a business that consisted of himself as the sole employee driving supplies around to his clients using the family car.

[13] It is possible that criminal elements have the potential to threaten and extort business owners and others generally in Hungary. While the panel accepts the fact that crime can be a problem in Hungary, just as it is in many nations, the state agencies in Hungary exist in order to, among other things, enforce the law and protect their citizens. The panel finds the principal claimant's fear is at the very least speculative and it finds that the fear itself is a risk (being of a victim of crime) that would be faced by any other citizen of Hungary who might open a business and who might encounter people who attempt to extort money from them. The panel finds the principal claimant is not a "person in need of protection". As his wife and two minor sons base their claims on that of the principal claimant, the panel also finds them not to be persons in need of protection.
The Minor Claimant's Mental Health Issues

[14] While in Canada, the claimants' eldest son, the minor claimant XXXX, suffered from mental issues resulting in his late-XXXX 2017 suicide attempt. The principal claimant wrote in his 'PIF Narrative Addition' that the young man's problems were caused by the events that happened in Hungary. The principal claimant said his son's suicide attempt occurred in XXXX 2017; however, the medical report9 from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXl Hospital confirms the son's hospitalization ("for acute suicidality") occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2017. He was discharged on XXXX XXXX, 2017. The principal claimant explained that his issues started when the claimants left Hungary and the incident in XXXX 2017 was a result of finding out that their refugee hearing 'would be coming up.' He said he attributes XXXX problems to being scared of going back home and that the problems they previously faced will start again.

[15] The panel finds that the objective documentary evidence and the testimony of the minor claimant XXXX do not support the principal claimant's allegation. In marked contrast to the principal claimant's testimony, XXXX testified on his own behalf regarding the cause of the mental and emotional issues he faced leading up to his attempted suicide in late XXXX 2017. He told the counsel and the panel that he had 'medical issues' before being hospitalized in XXXX, although he had never previously sought professional help. He attributed his problems to pressure he was experiencing in school in Canada and specifically, to the pressure he was placing on himself to do well in school. He said that he was doing 'a lot more tests' in chemistry, biology, mathematics and English and the pressure he was experiencing was such that he dropped all of his school subjects. He was clear with the panel and his counsel when he stated that the school work and pressure he put on himself became too much, resulting in his suicide attempt. He said he felt a 'whole load of pressure' lifted off his shoulders after he dropped the courses.

[16] By extension, neither of the medical documents submitted to corroborate XXXX personal situation10 link the reason for his mental collapse to his father's alleged business trouble in Hungary with mafia types trying to extort money from him. For example, the doctor's discharge diagnosis is "Social anxiety disorder, ADD, rule out learning disability." The doctor also referenced XXXX "unrestricted access to video gaming interfering with sleep onset and sleep maintenance" as a factor in treating the boy during his hospitalization. The reporting doctor also noted he took a family history from the two adult claimants and noted that XXXX screening testing came back "clinically significant for ADD." Further, the doctor opined in his report that he is "not certain if anxiety is free-standing social anxiety or actually comorbid or untreated ADD; however, focus of this admission will be treatment of anxiety". Moreover, the doctor recorded the minor claimant's reference to "years of introverted coping style, insecurities, social phobias, social avoidance and isolation." Such diagnoses clearly pre-date any reference to the principal claimant's allegations of several incidents that compelled him to close his business and leave Hungary. In fact, there is no persuasive evidence before the panel - including in the medical evidence - that links XXXX medical issues to what the principal claimant experienced. The panel prefers the medical evidence and XXXX own admission as to the reasons for his medical issues to that of the principal claimant who, the panel finds, sought to use the young man's attempted suicide and hospitalization in XXXX 2017 to establish a subjective fear of criminal elements in Hungary. The panel is not persuaded by the principal claimant's evidence as stated. Further, XXXX testified that he would feel worse if he returned to Hungary as the health care in Hungary is not as good as Canada's health care system. He said he would feel even more depressed and anxious especially since he is accustomed to life in Canada. At no time during the hearing did he offer evidence that his situation stems from any issues that his father and/or the family faced in Hungary.

[17] On this point, the panel observed carefully XXXX comportment and manner of testifying. Just as the doctor reported in his observations, the panel also finds XXXX to be a coherent and responsive witness. He testified as a well-spoken and articulate young man who answered all questions put to him by both his counsel and the panel. The panel noted on the record that XXXXappears to be an intelligent and thoughtful person. He answered all questions put to him carefully and his answers were spontaneous and unrehearsed. The panel finds XXXX to be highly credible regarding the reasons for his past mental issues.

[18] Coupled with the fact that the medical documents are silent on any reference to the principal claimant's alleged problems impacting XXXX, and considering XXXX own oral testimony, which is very specific as to his understanding of the scholastic pressures that caused his breakdown and suicide attempt, the panel is persuaded that this young man told the panel the truth; that the XXXX 2017 incident and his hospitalization for XXXX days was directly attributable to the pressure he felt from his school work and the tests he was taking, along with the pressure he exerted upon himself to excel scholastically - and his problems do not stem from the principal claimant's prior extortion and business issues with XXXX and his cohorts. Accordingly, as much as the panel would like to assuage this minor claimant's anxiety regarding having to return to Hungary, the panel is bound by the narrow confines of two specific sections of the IRPA. Given that the claimants are not Convention refugees, the harm they face, if any, is a risk that would be faced generally by all persons in Hungary who would be targeted by criminals. The panel finds that these claimants are not persons in need of protection and they do not face a particular risk that would take them out of the realm of the exception in Section 97(1)(b)(ii).
The Submissions of the Claimants' Counsel

[19] Through his submissions, the claimants' counsel sought to broaden the definition of membership in a particular social group by defining the claimants as "business people and their families who are targeted by criminals without police protection causing those affected to leave the country." The panel does not accept as persuasive this submission. This submission and the proposed appellation are not supported by the category of "particular social group" as set out in Ward11, which identifies the three categories (see below as referenced in Cius v. Canada, (2008) FC 1) - and none of these three permit the principal claimant and his family to shelter.

[20] In the panel's determination, the counsel's submission has been precisely and clearly addressed in Canadian jurisprudence. For example, in paragraph 20 of Cius12: "It is clear from the Court's reference to Ward, above, that the protection afforded under the Convention is intended to provide protection on the grounds of human rights and anti-discrimination considerations, and not general criminality." In the case at hand, the principal claimant himself would not be marginalized or discriminated against as a returnee. Rather, according to counsel, the principal claimant would be targeted by criminal elements based on an alleged bounty put out on him if he returned to Hungary after five years abroad in Canada. On this point, the Canadian jurisprudence is also clearly established in the Barthelemy and Cius13 decisions, amongst others:
Barthelemy
"[19] ...It is settled law that a fear of criminal assaults does not constitute, in itself, persecution linked to one of the five Convention grounds. ...

[20] The same finding applies to the applicant's claim based on her membership in the Haitian diaspora and to the risk if she were to return. The RPD was correct in finding that this was not a case of a particular social group for the purposes of section 96 and that fear of persecution based on this characteristic had no nexus to one of the five Convention grounds (see, among others, the two decisions cited by the RPD on this point, namely Prophète v. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, 2008 FC 331 (CanLII), 2008 FC 331, at paragraphs 20-21, 167 A.C.W.S. (3d) 151 and Cius v. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, 2008 FC 1 (CanLII), 2008 FC 1 at paragraph 23, [2008] F.C.J. No. 9 (QL); see also: Soimin v. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, 2009 FC 218 (CanLII), 2009 FC 218, [2009] F.C.J. No. 246 (QL)).14
Cius15
"[14]... In making this argument, the applicant relies on the definition of "particular social group" adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada in Ward, above. The relevant passage is the following (at para. 70):
The meaning assigned to "particular social group" in the Act should take into account the general underlying themes of the defence of human rights and anti-discrimination that form the basis for the international refugee protection initiative. The tests proposed in Mayers, supra, Cheung, supra, and Matter of Acosta, supra, provide a good working rule to achieve this result. They identify three possible categories:
(1) groups defined by an innate or unchangeable characteristic;
(2) groups whose members voluntarily associate for reasons so fundamental to their human dignity that they should not be forced to forsake the association; and
(3) groups associated by a former voluntary status, unalterable due to its historical permanence.
The first category would embrace individuals fearing persecution on such bases as gender, linguistic background and sexual orientation, while the second would encompass, for example, human rights activists. The third branch is included more because of historical intentions, although it is also relevant to the anti-discrimination influences, in that one's past is an immutable part of the person.
....

[18] The violence to which the applicant might be subject is generalized. It is the fallout of criminal activity, and not the targeting of a particular group in a discriminatory fashion. As a group, people who are perceived to be wealthy are not marginalized in Haiti; rather they are more frequent targets of criminal activity. The perception of wealth is insufficient to sustain the position that Haitian returnees constitute a social group16.

[19] The harm feared is criminal in nature, and has no nexus to the Convention refugee definition. In a recent decision Étienne v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [2007] F.C.J. No. 99 (QL), 2007 FC 64, Justice Shore dealt with the argument that wealth constitutes a particular social group:

[15] Mr. Étienne's allegation, that the Board erred when it determined, that his claim provided no nexus to a Convention ground as required under section 96 of IRPA, is unfounded. The Board was justified in concluding that gaining wealth or winning a lottery does not constitute membership in a particular social group.

[16] In Moali de Sanchez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 183, [2001] F.C.J. No. 375, Justice Yvon Pinard rejected the extended interpretation of the concept of a social group:

[6] I also find that the RD's second conclusion is free of error. In Canada (Attorney General) v. Ward, [1993] 2 S.C.R. 689, the Supreme Court of Canada rejected the extended interpretation of the concept of a social group. The status of a landed proprietor does not in any way fall within the "general underlying themes of the defence of human rights and anti-discrimination" (Ward, supra, at 739) and is not a "characteristic of personhood not alterable by conscious action and in some cases not alterable except on the basis of unacceptable costs" (Ward, supra, at 738). The tribunal also referred to Wilcox v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), November 2, 1993, [1993] F.C.J. No. 1157, A-1282-92, in which Reed J. found as follows at paras. [3]:
I interpret the Tribunal's decision as finding that there was no evidence that the Peruvian upper middle class is subject to any greater level of (what the Tribunal referred to as) depredation than others in Peruvian society generally. I interpret the Tribunal's decision as finding that the Sendero Luminosa are raining terror on everyone in Peru. While the type of danger which the applicants fear (extortion) may only be operative against the rich, this does not mean that the applicants have been or will be subject to persecution in the convention refugee sense. [Emphasis added]17

[21] "It is clear from the Court's reference to Ward, above, that the protection afforded under the Convention is intended to provide protection on the grounds of human rights and anti-discrimination considerations, and not general criminality."18 The panel finds that a small business owner facing criminality in Hungary does not constitute membership in a particular social group within the meaning of s. 96 of the Act.

[22] With respect to the allegations of being targeted by criminals in general in Hungary, in this subsection of its analysis, the panel has examined the question of the principal claimant's risk vis-à-vis criminals in Hungary. The panel also examined whether the principal claimant, as a business person targeted by mafia, faces a generalized risk vis-à-vis criminals in general in Hungary, or whether he faces a particular risk that would take him out of the realm of the exception in Section 97(1)(b)(ii).

[23] With respect to the claimant's risk vis-à-vis criminals in general in Hungary, the panel considered the jurisprudence found in Prophète where at paragraph 23, the Court states:
Based on the recent jurisprudence of this Court, I am of the view that the applicant does not face a personalized risk that is not faced generally by other individuals in or from Haiti. The risk of all forms of criminality is general and felt by all Haitians. While a specific number of individuals may be targeted more frequently because of their wealth, all Haitians are at risk of becoming the victims of violence.19

[24] The jurisprudence in this instance supports the conclusion that this case is one of generalized risk as far as criminals in Hungary are concerned. The panel also finds that the principal claimant has not demonstrated how the risk in his particular circumstances would be different than other Hungarian as far as criminality in Hungary is concerned.

[25] Given the testimony in this case, as well as the jurisprudence and the aforementioned stated reasons, the panel finds that, according to section 97(1)(b)(ii) of the Act, the principal claimant and his family face a generalized risk as far as criminals in general within Hungary are concerned, and therefore they are not considered "persons in need of protection" should they return to that country.

[26] With respect to the counsel's submission that the harm faced by the minor claimant extends to all the claimants, the panel finds this submission to be unpersuasive. The counsel submitted that the panel must consider that the risk to XXXX is not a generalized risk because it impacts his "mental well-being and health". In Baires Sanchez20, Justice Crampton stated that in order to show that a risk is not generalized, applicants must "establish that the risk of actual or threatened similar violence is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country." And that applicants must demonstrate that the respective risks that they face are not prevalent or widespread in their respective countries of origin, in the sense of being a risk faced by a significant subset of the population.

[27] One of the leading cases on this matter is Portillo21, in which the Federal Court articulated a two-step test for determining generalized versus personalized test. The Board must first appropriately determine the nature of the risk faced by the claimant, which requires an assessment of whether the claimant faces an ongoing or future risk, what that risk is, whether it is one of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment and the basis for the risk. Second, the correctly described risk faced by the claimant must then be compared to that faced by a significant group in the country at issue to determine whether the risks are of the same nature and degree. As well, it will typically be the case that where an individual is subject to a personal risk to his life or risks cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, then that risk is no longer general.

[28] In this context, the panel finds that the harm faced by XXXX is not demonstrative of a personalized risk that lies outside of generalized risk faced by others in Hungary. First, the panel considered carefully the best interests of the affected minor claimant XXXX as a person who has experienced, and who has been treated for, mental health issues. The panel considered the medical reports and the minor claimant's current restorative treatment regimen with, among other things, medication and social worker interaction and in the context of his straightforward testimony. None of this evidence or testimony references criminal experiences or the principal claimant's alleged run-ins with the mafia in Hungary. Unlike the decision of Kanthasamy22 as the counsel referenced as being applicable, the panel distinguishes the case at bar from that case. Here, the panel has considered carefully and placed significant weight on both the contents of the medical reports and XXXX testimony. Further, the panel went on in this case to consider what future harm or risk the minor claimant might face and in the context of the counsel's submission that the harm is not generalized but that XXXX and his family face a personalized risk.

[29] The panel has already determined that the harm faced by these claimants is a generalized risk based on the principal claimant's former status as a small business person targeted for criminal reasons, which is not a Convention ground. The panel considered whether other individuals in Hungary face the same risk generally, which they do when they are targeted by criminal elements. The panel considered whether the risks are of the same nature and degree; that is, the forward-looking component of the harm feared should XXXX and his family return to Hungary (as the counsel asked the panel to consider that XXXX mental health issues impacts the family as a whole returning to that country).

[30] XXXX expressed a concern about the health care he might receive upon return to Hungary although there is no basis for his concern because the XXXX-year-old never testified to any personal or general experiences with the Hungarian health care system let alone never testified to having received inadequate care; the adult claimant's materials made no reference to the system in their written or oral evidence; and the claimants' counsel offered no submissions in this regard. The minor claimant's statement is speculative at best. As noted in the Board's "Consolidated Grounds in the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act: Persons in Need of Protection - Risk to Life or Risk of Cruel and Unusual Treatment or Punishment" of May 15, 2002 ("Consolidated Grounds"), Section 3.1.9 is instructive:
3.1.9 Risk Not Due to Inadequate Health or Medical Care
If the risk is caused by the inability of the country of reference to provide adequate health or medical care the claimant will not qualify for protection. A similar requirement in the PRDCC Regulations was explained in the PDRCC Guidelines as reflecting the position that the Regulations were never intended to compensate for disparities between the health and medical care available in Canada and those available elsewhere in the world. The same could be said of s. 97(1)(b)(iv).23

[31] The risk faced by XXXX is not caused by inadequate health or medical care in Hungary. The panel also relied upon the referenced decision of Bensaid24, referenced and contained in section "4.5.1.5 Medical Treatment" of the Board's "Consolidated Grounds" in assessing the minor claimant's allegation that inadequate health care would be available to him in Hungary. Bensaid concerned the expulsion of an Algerian, following findings by immigration officials that his indefinite leave to remain in the U.K. had been obtained by deception, his marriage being one of convenience. The applicant was a schizophrenic suffering from long-term mental illness. He argued that his expulsion would result in a relapse and the deterioration of his condition due to the difficulties obtaining medicine, and the stresses and violence involved with living in an area where there was active terrorism. "While the Court recognized that, in principle, an expulsion with such consequences could violate Article 3, in this case, the risks were purely speculative."

[32] The inability of a country to provide adequate health or medical care generally can be distinguished from those situations where adequate health or medical care is provided to some individuals but not to others. The individuals who are denied treatment may be able to establish a claim under s. 97(1)(b) because in their case, their risk arises from the country's unwillingness to provide them with adequate care. These types of situations may also succeed under the refugee ground if the risk is associated with one of the Convention reasons. In this case, however, neither the minor claimant nor the adult claimants have established that the minor claimant will not be provided adequate health or medical care for his issues - all of which the panel finds stem from reasons other than the principal claimant's situation.

[33] The panel then analyzed whether in this case, where risk is alleged, that risk arises not because of the lack of adequate health and medical care, but because the person has a medical condition that will make him or her more vulnerable to the unstable conditions in his or her country as the claimants' counsel submitted. This was in fact the situation in Ahmed25 where the applicant suffered from schizophrenia. Unlike XXXX, this claimant had no family or support in his country and this made him, given his condition, very vulnerable due to the instability in Somalia. The Federal Court directed that the risk to the applicant's life be assessed in light of his medical condition, and not from the perspective of a lack of availability of adequate medical care. In the case at bar, the minor claimant will be returning to Hungary with his immediate family members who have provided him with care and support in Canada. There are no persuasive reasons to doubt that XXXX parents and his brother will not continue to provide that same care and support to him as a family unit in Hungary. The claimants also furnished no persuasive evidence that the impact on XXXX would be such that he faces any greater harm than they would face if they return to Hungary.

[34] Once more, unlike Kanthasamy26, wherein the Supreme Court found that an H&C officer had unreasonably assessed a psychologist's report about the applicant's mental health, the panel in this case finds persuasive the medical diagnosis XXXX presented at this hearing that was stated in these reasons in paragraphs 15 and 16. However, neither of the adult claimants, nor XXXX himself, has provided evidence that he would be unable to obtain adequate health and medical care if required in their native Hungary, or that in returning to Hungary, it would amount to hardship that is unusual and undeserved or disproportionate. As in Kanthasamy27, the panel has considered the effect of removal from Canada on XXXX mental health. The panel has no medically-supported diagnosis before it to establish a heightened risk for the minor claimant if he returns to Hungary. Further, "no evidence has been provided to satisfy [the panel] that his family would be "unable or unwilling to assist or support him with reintegration into [Hungarian] society." By extension, as someone fast approaching adulthood on his imminent XXXX birthday, the minor claimant has recovered, he is in treatment and he has returned to his academic studies in Canada. There is no evidence before the panel to show that XXXX would be unable to attend school, pursue post-secondary studies, or otherwise obtain employment upon his return to Hungary, or that supportive care would not be available to him. And, the panel finds that if there is any impact on his mental well-being if he returned to Hungary, the evidence adduced at this hearing has not demonstrated that the impact would arise from the principal claimant's situation, or for any Convention ground.

[35] The claimants' counsel also referenced the decision of Lohazyak28 wherein the reviewing officer ignored the effect of removal from Canada on the principal applicant, his wife and son. That effect was contained in a psychological assessment provided by a Canadian practitioner who warned about the impacts of return on the applicants. No such evidence was presented at this hearing and unlike in Lohazyak, the panel in this case has referenced the persuasive weight it assigns to the medical reports and XXXX testimony about his circumstances and history - However, the problems that the minor claimant experienced in Canada stem from reasons other than the principal claimant's issues with someone who allegedly extorted money from him in Hungary. Moreover, there was no persuasive testimony presented at this hearing to establish any negative impact on XXXX if he returned to Hungary beyond his statement that he feared that his problems would reoccur if he left Canada. The panel finds that XXXX return to Hungary - and by extension that proffered by his counsel for all the claimants - is not appropriately characterized as a personalized risk. There is nothing particular in their experiences in Canada or in XXXX particular circumstances that make them vulnerable to anything more than a generalized risk if they return to Hungary.

[36] The claimants' counsel proffered general submissions on country conditions in Hungary despite acknowledging that the panel had not asked for such submissions. After its analysis of the counsel's document references, the panel finds no persuasive evidence before it to establish that conditions in Hungary are such that XXXX and the other claimants would be subject to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture should they return to Hungary. The risk these claimants face, if at all, is the risk that would be faced generally by persons in every part of that country who had been targeted by criminal elements. And, in this case, the principal claimant and his family left Hungary more than five years ago and the panel finds that they are not at risk of being targeted by mafia elements today. It is important to re-state that the panel was not persuaded by the principal claimant's attempt to link his son's mental issues with his own problems with XXXX and his cohorts. Today, having spent more than five years outside of their country of nationality, the panel expects that it will take some time for the claimants to re-adapt and re-integrate into life in Hungary and that, as in Lohazyak29, there will be "a period of social and economic adjustment when they first return to [Hungary], which would likely result in some hardship for them." Moreover, the panel considered the particular circumstances of XXXX and the effect of what his removal from Canada might be on his mental health. Specifically, the panel identified, assessed and weighed the effect of his return to Hungary with his family based on the evidence. The panel is not persuaded that further psychological harm will be caused to the minor claimant if he returns to Hungary and no medical or other evidence before the panel supports such a claim. The best interests of the minor claimant have been carefully considered and assessed against all of the evidence in this case, the panel finds that his removal along with the other claimants will not create any greater harm or impact upon him.

[37] Lastly, the claimants' counsel expanded the definition of a particular social group by identifying the claimants as "not only the family left the country of origin but one of its members has an acute mental health issue". For the jurisprudential reasons referenced in paragraphs 19 through 24 of these reasons, the panel places no weight on such a broadening of the term "particular social group." The panel cannot assign weight to the reliance of the principal claimant, the female claimant and the other minor claimant on a risk that XXXX might face if the family returns to Hungary.
CONCLUSION

[38] As the claimants are not Convention refugees, in that they have failed to establish a nexus to any Convention ground, they are deemed to be persons who are not in need of protection. In this regard, the panel finds they will not be subject to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture should they return to Hungary. The risk they face, if at all, is the risk that would be faced generally by persons in every part of that country.

[39] For these reasons, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX(the principal claimant), his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX(the female claimant) and their two sons XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX(minor claimants), are not Convention refugees. Their claims are rejected.
